title: Pronouns
intro: Make clear who or what a pronoun refers to.

sections.heading: Subjective vs. objective case
body: Use I, he, she, we, they, or who as a subject: the person or thing doing or being something. Use me, him, her, us, them, or whom as an object: the person or thing receiving an action or following a word such as to or with.
In a compound phrase, remove the other name to check case: “went to Maria and I” becomes “went to I,” so use me. After a preposition, use the object form: between you and me.

examples.text: She and her brother painted the fence.
examples.label: Subjects use subjective case

examples.text: The coach thanked her and me after the game.
examples.label: Objects use objective case

examples.text: The coach thanked she and I after the game.
examples.label: Wrong case for objects

sections.tip: Cover the other noun and the conjunction, then read the pronoun by itself. Your ear will catch the error.

sections.heading: Who vs. whom
body: Look at the pronoun’s job in its own clause. Try he and him in that part of the sentence. If he fits, use who; if him fits, use whom. “The conductor chose him” gives “the violinist whom the conductor chose.”
Do the same for whoever/whomever. In “to whoever finishes first,” whoever is the subject of finishes; the preceding to does not make it an object inside that clause.

examples.text: The scientist who discovered the enzyme will speak.
examples.label: who = subject (she discovered)

examples.text: The violinist whom the conductor chose played first.
examples.label: whom = object (chose her)

examples.text: The prize goes to whoever finishes first.
examples.label: whoever = subject of 'finishes,' even after 'to'

sections.tip: Replace the clause with he/him. He = who, him = whom.

sections.heading: Pronoun-antecedent agreement
body: Find the noun the pronoun replaces; this is its antecedent. Keep the reference clear and check whether it means one or more than one. Each, either, neither, anyone, and everyone take singular verbs. An “of the…” phrase between subject and verb does not change that.

A committee or team acting as one unit takes its. For neither X nor Y, check the nearer noun and avoid an unclear reference. For a person, judge the pronoun in context rather than by an isolated noun alone.

examples.text: Each of the laptops comes with its own charger.
examples.label: 'Each' is singular — 'of the laptops' doesn't change that

examples.text: Each of the laptops comes with their own charger.
examples.label: Plural pronoun, singular antecedent

sections.tip: Find the exact noun the pronoun replaces, then make the number match. Cross out the prepositional phrase in between.

sections.heading: Ambiguous pronoun reference
body: If a pronoun could point to two nouns, name the one you mean. “Lena set the vase on the shelf, and it cracked” could mean the vase or the shelf.
A longer choice can be better when it removes ambiguity: “the shelf cracked.” Check especially for nearby people or objects that could share the same pronoun.

examples.text: When Lena set the vase on the shelf, the shelf cracked.
examples.label: Noun removes ambiguity

examples.text: When Lena set the vase on the shelf, it cracked.
examples.label: 'it' could mean two nouns

sections.tip: If you have to pause and ask 'which one?', pick the choice that names the noun outright.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: I/me or who/whom choices ask about the pronoun’s job. Its/their asks what it refers to. It’s and they’re are contractions: shortened forms of it is and they are. A specific noun may make an unclear reference clear.
Find the noun being replaced, check the pronoun’s job, and make sure its reference is clear. Expand a contraction into its full words before deciding it shows ownership.
sections.tip: On ambiguity questions, the one choice that repeats the noun usually wins. Clarity beats brevity when a pronoun could point two ways.

check.stem: The director offered the lead role to Carla and [[I]].
check.explanation: The pronoun is the object of the preposition 'to,' so 'me' is correct — drop 'Carla and' and read 'offered the lead role to me.' 'I' is a subject pronoun, 'myself' is reflexive and has no matching subject 'I' in the sentence, and 'mine' is possessive.

check.stem: The author [[who]] the panel honored thanked her readers.
check.explanation: Inside the clause, the panel honored her — the pronoun receives the action, so 'whom' is correct. 'Who' is the subject form, 'which' refers to things rather than people, and 'that whom' stacks two relative pronouns into an ungrammatical pair.

check.stem: Each of the branch offices manages [[their]] own budget.
check.explanation: The antecedent is 'each,' which is singular — 'of the branch offices' is a prepositional phrase that does not change the number — so the singular possessive 'its' agrees. 'Their' is plural, 'it's' means 'it is,' and 'they're' means 'they are'; neither contraction can show possession.
